title: The New Sobriety About Reading 2026
author: Robert Pondiscio
source: The Next 30 Years (Substack) / Thomas B. Fordham Institute's Education Gadfly, August 6,
summary: Robert Pondiscio argues that a subtle but significant shift is underway in the national conversation about reading education. He points to near-simultaneous essays in The New York Times (James Traub) and The Atlantic (Adam Kirsch) that evaluated Texas's controversial statewide curriculum and Bible-inclusive reading list on educational merits rather than culture-war terms, both invoking E.D. Hirsch's theory of cultural literacy. He connects this to The Atlantic's widely discussed cover story by Rose Horowitch on the broader collapse of sustained reading in American life, and to the multi-year 'science of reading' movement sparked by Emily Hanford's reporting, which discredited balanced literacy and three-cueing instruction. Pondiscio contends that mounting evidence of reading failure is eroding confidence in decades of 'student-centered,' skills-based, choice-driven pedagogy and reviving older ideas: common curricula, sequenced knowledge-building, and adult-directed text selection. He frames this as a possible end to education's 'postmodern moment,' though he stops short of declaring a full trend based on just a few data points. The piece was originally published in the Thomas B. Fordham Institute's Education Gadfly newsletter.
points: The Atlantic and New York Times opinion sections both published essays evaluating Texas's Bible-inclusive curriculum on educational rather than political grounds.
Both essays invoke E.D. Hirsch's cultural literacy framework, arguing that shared background knowledge is essential to reading comprehension.

Rose Horowitch's Atlantic cover story on the decline of reading — including the finding that Americans now gamble more than they read for leisure — has amplified concern about a 'civilizational risk.'

Emily Hanford's reporting on the science of reading discredited balanced literacy and three-cueing, prompting states to mandate phonics-based instruction and shifting debate toward comprehension-building.
Pondiscio argues these developments may signal the erosion of education's 'postmodern moment,' though he is cautious about declaring a full trend.
quotes: During my years at TIME magazine, the newsroom had a rule of thumb: If something happens once, it's news. Twice is a coincidence. Three times? That's a trend.
we become good readers "by acquiring the vocabulary, grammatical knowledge and stock of information that allow us to make sense of a text.

for a high school graduate not to know about the parting of the Red Sea or the Sermon on the Mount is a disadvantage, for the same reason that not knowing about the Puritans or the Civil War is a disadvantage
Call it a vibe shift, or perhaps simply a new sobriety about reading and what it will take to arrest its long decline.
we are now more likely to spend leisure time gambling than reading books—a statistic that would have sounded absurd a generation ago.
What's at risk," she writes, "is nothing less than the ability to think for oneself.
Parents who had never heard the phrase "three-cueing" suddenly knew exactly what it meant and why it's not a very good way to learn to read.
Maybe a common curriculum is not a tool of oppression but an instrument of democratic inheritance and equity.
By the time everyone recognizes that a trend exists, it's usually been underway for quite some time.
